analysis.one_liner: Gives state attorneys general power to sue police departments for patterns of misconduct.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee after being referred there in June 2021, dying without a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let state attorneys general, not just the federal Justice Department, sue state and local police agencies in federal court when they engage in patterns or practices of unconstitutional conduct. It would add $445 million a year for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division (at least $100 million of it for this kind of enforcement), create a $150 million-a-year grant program to help states investigate police misconduct, and require that court-approved police reform agreements include community oversight bodies made up of people who have never worked in law enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of communities where police departments show repeated patterns of unconstitutional conduct, including through the requirement that reform agreements include mental health support, restorative justice programs, and community oversight bodies made up of non-law-enforcement members.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People in communities with patterns of police misconduct

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives state attorneys general independent authority to bring federal civil suits to eliminate patterns or practices of unconstitutional police conduct, so enforcement would not depend solely on the Justice Department, which can change priorities with each administration.

It requires consent decrees and settlement agreements to include remedies beyond police reforms, such as mental health support and community-based restorative justice, and to incorporate community oversight bodies with the power to question agencies, obtain documents, and recommend changes.

It authorizes $445 million per fiscal year (2021-2030) for the DOJ Civil Rights Division, with at least $100 million each year reserved for pattern-or-practice enforcement and technical assistance, plus a separate $150 million per year grant program for states pursuing such cases.

It extends the pattern-or-practice prohibition to prosecutors, courts, and other justice agencies, and blocks a conflicted official from leading a state investigation, requiring an independent organization when a statewide office is under investigation.

analysis.who_pays: Police agencies and governments that would face more lawsuits, court-ordered reforms, community oversight bodies, and reporting requirements; the cost of new programs would fall on federal appropriations.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes roughly $595 million per year in new federal spending over ten years, which would need annual appropriations and adds to federal outlays.

State attorneys general suing their own state's agencies could create political conflicts, which is why the bill builds conflict-of-interest screens and requires an independent organization when a statewide office is investigated, but critics could still question the design.
Grant eligibility requires states to commit to community-based programs that reduce reliance on law enforcement, a condition some states would reject, potentially limiting participation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a structural enforcement expansion: it creates a second, independent layer of oversight over police misconduct and pushes reform agreements toward community-based remedies. The cost is new federal spending and more litigation exposure for police agencies. The main weakness is that it was written to supplement, not guarantee, enforcement: its protections depend on willing state attorneys general and continued federal funding.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2021, and the committee took no further action on it before the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on June 9, 2021, joined by 10 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was taken: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

The bill's provisions would have expanded pattern-or-practice enforcement authority to state attorneys general, funded DOJ Civil Rights Division enforcement at $445 million per year, created a state grant program, and required community oversight bodies in consent decrees.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Police agencies and local governments that would have faced state-level pattern-or-practice lawsuits and community oversight requirements are better off because the bill never advanced; ordinary residents in jurisdictions with patterns of misconduct remain without the additional enforcement route the bill would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that avoided added lawsuits and oversight

for.name: Edward Markey, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Van Hollen, Mazie Hirono, Tammy Duckworth, Richard Blumenthal, Kirsten Gillibrand, Bernie Sanders, and Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; Sanders caucuses as an independent.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (Chair Dick Durbin)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 initial supporters were Democrats or allied independents (9 of 48 Senate Democrats and 1 of 2 independents); no Republican cosponsor joined, and the Democratic-led Judiciary Committee never scheduled action.

industries.industry: State and local law enforcement agencies and their unions
industries.note: The bill would expose police agencies to lawsuits from state attorneys general, court-ordered consent decrees with community oversight bodies, and grants conditioned on reducing reliance on policing. These agencies' interest in avoiding external oversight runs against the bill's aim of protecting residents from patterns of unconstitutional conduct.

industries.industry: DOJ Civil Rights Division and state attorney general offices
industries.note: The bill would fund federal civil rights enforcement at $445 million per year and empower state AGs with new litigation authority and grants. Its success would depend on these offices, which the bill positions as the permanent enforcement channel alongside federal DOJ.
